title: The first screen of a client portal
metaTitle: The file a client was promised
excerpt: The first screen of a client portal should be the file the client was promised, with one action to open it. A tour of the portal makes them hunt for what you said was ready.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, a front door you can pick out before you learn the whole plan.
caption: The entrance should be the part they were told to use. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a client see first in a portal?
faqs.answer: The file they were promised, named the way the email named it, with one action to open or download it. If several files are ready, the newest promised file comes first, with the date and who updated it. A tour of the portal, a phase dashboard, and a welcome video make them hunt for the thing you said was already there.

faqs.question: What if nothing has been shared yet?
faqs.answer: Say that plainly. No file is ready yet, and say what will appear, such as brand files, documents, or a project update. Do not show an empty dashboard that looks broken. An honest empty state is a better first screen than a tour of features they cannot use until the first file lands.

faqs.question: Should the portal open on a project overview?
faqs.answer: Only if the overview is the thing they were promised. Most clients who click a link are looking for a file or an update, not a map of your process. Put the overview behind the file, or under it. The first view should match the sentence in the email that brought them.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Client portal UX on the first screen is a promise about a file. A client looking for the file they were promised should see that object and one action. Open it, or download it. A tour of the portal makes them hunt for something you already said was ready.

The object is the logo pack, the document, or the update you named in the email. The action is to open it. If the screen is a dashboard of phases, they will assume the file is somewhere inside a phase, and they will be annoyed before they have read a word of the work.

## They came from a sentence, not from a map

The email said the files were in the portal. The first screen has to cash that sentence. Same noun as the email. If you wrote "brand files," the screen says brand files, not "asset library" and not "deliverable 04." The client did not learn your internal filing system. They learned the sentence you sent.

On a Hanabi project, the portal is where brand files, documents, and updates live after delivery. That is the job of the first screen too: the latest thing they were told exists, in front, with a way to open it. The rest of the archive can sit behind it. The archive is not the greeting.

Jakob Nielsen, writing for the Nielsen Norman Group, reported that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear in the first 10. A client with a meeting in an hour is a sharp case of that finding. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is what to show anyone who wants a product walkthrough before the download. The walkthrough can wait. The file cannot.

If they are new and nothing is shared yet, the object is that fact. "Nothing is here yet. Brand files and project updates will show up on this screen." That is a complete first view. An empty chart of milestones looks like a broken login.

## Name the file the way you named it in the email

Pick one file as the hero when one file is the news. The title, the date, and who placed it there. Open or Download as the action, depending on what you actually support. If both work, pick the one they need for the meeting and make the other secondary. Two equal buttons are a small tax. A single obvious one is better when they are in a hurry.

When several files landed together, list them under a heading that repeats the email. "Files shared on Tuesday." The newest, or the one you called out by name, is first. Do not sort alphabetically if the email called out a specific document. Alphabetical is how "Zoning notes" buries "Homepage copy."

Use the filename they will recognize, plus a human title if the filename is ugly. "Homepage copy" with the file name in smaller type is kind. A uuid with a download icon is a scavenger hunt. They will download three wrong files before the call.

Version in the title if versions are how you work. "Logo pack, current" beats a folder of final, final-2, and final-FINAL. If an older file must stay, label it older and tuck it under the current one. The first screen shows current. History is one tap away, not the top of the page.

One noun from the email to the button to the success. If the email said logo pack, the button says Open logo pack, and the opened file is that pack. "View resource" is a different product. The client does not have resources. They have the file you promised.

## One action, then the rest of the portal

The action opens the file. It does not start a tour, and it does not require them to complete a profile. You already know who they are if the link was signed. If they must sign in, the screen after sign-in is still the file, not a home they must cross.

Do not gate the download behind a questionnaire about how they heard of you. Do not gate it behind an orientation checklist. They are trying to keep a promise to their own team. Your checklist is an interruption of that promise.

A short line of context is allowed when the file needs it. "This replaces the pack from last Friday." That line prevents them from presenting the wrong marks. It is not a tour. A tour points at the sidebar, the search box, and the notification bell. They do not need those until the file is in their hands.

If the file is large, say so before they tap, in words. "Large file. Downloading may take a minute." Then let the tap start the download. A surprise multi-hundred-megabyte fetch on a phone in a lobby is how the first screen fails even when the link was right.

Comments, approvals, and status can live on the file, under the action, if the work genuinely needs a response. "Approved" is a second action with a different job. Do not make approval the only way to open the file. People need to read before they approve. Reading is the first action.

## What a tour and a phase board cost

A phase board answers "where is the project." Sometimes that is the question. Often the question is "where is the file you just mentioned." If you always open on phases, you have chosen your question over theirs.

Put phases, if you have them, behind or beneath the new files. A client who wants the map can open it. A client who wants the PDF should not have to learn the map. The first screen that teaches your process before it delivers the work feels like the work is still being withheld.

Welcome videos and coach marks cover the filename. Count the taps from the email link to a visible file name. Zero is the goal. One is acceptable if they must choose between two projects. More than one means the portal is introducing itself instead of keeping the promise.

Motion before the file list is the same delay. Show the name immediately, even if the preview takes a moment. A skeleton in the shape of the filename is fine. A full-screen brand animation is a strange thing to make a client watch on the way to their own logo.

## What to leave off the first view

Leave the studio's internal task list off. Leave invoices off unless the email was about an invoice. Leave a feed of every comment ever made off the top. The newest file, then the activity that belongs to it.

Leave other clients' work off, obviously, and also leave other projects of the same client collapsed if the link was about one project. A switcher can exist. It should not be the first decision if the link already chose.

Leave "complete your company profile" off this screen. A missing phone number does not block a PDF. Ask for extras when you need them, on the action that needs them. The first open is not that action.

If you want the screen to feel substantial, substance is the file and the date. A large empty hero with a stock photograph of a handshake makes the real filename smaller. Give the filename the hero's space.


A signed link and a bookmarked home should resolve to the same file once the client is identified. Teams often polish the link in the email and forget the bookmark. The client who returns next week uses the bookmark. They should not get a thinner portal because they came back without the original message. Same noun, same first file, both paths.

Previews that ask for a second sign-in inside a frame will be reported as a missing file. If the preview cannot share the portal session, skip the preview and offer the download. A preview that fails closed looks like a permission problem, and you will spend the permission sentence on an embedding bug. Save that sentence for a file that is actually withheld. The client can tell the difference only if you can.
## Review it from the email

Send the real email to a test client. Open it on a phone. After sign-in, you should see the noun from the subject line without scrolling. Tap once. The file opens or downloads. If you land on a dashboard and have to remember which phase contains "brand," the first screen is wrong.

Repeat with no files shared. The sentence should be calm and specific, not a zero-state illustration with no next step. Repeat with two projects. The link's project should already be selected.

Then break the open. Expired link, failed preview, wrong account. The next piece is [errors in a client portal](/blog/errors-in-a-client-portal). A first screen that only works for the person who built it, already signed in, on the office network, has not met the client yet.

When you want to see a portal treated as part of the work and not as a separate gadget, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The first screen should feel like the email, kept.
